However, much of the anger directed at Martin stemmed from the fact that his office also oversees the handling of expense claims. Critics contend that he allowed such claims to spiral out of control and failed to grasp the extent of public outrage over sums that, in some cases, reached into the tens of thousands of dollars.

Politicians across the political spectrum have come under scrutiny following weeks of front-page revelations about their expense claims—including requests for reimbursement on mortgages that had already been paid off, multiple members of the same family claiming identical expenses, and reimbursements for extravagant home furnishings.

# London: A City Where History Meets the Future

LONDON, England (CNN) — Few cities in the world carry the weight of history quite like London. As the capital of the United Kingdom, this sprawling metropolis on the banks of the River Thames has witnessed centuries of transformation, from Roman settlement to medieval stronghold, from imperial capital to modern global hub.

Walking through London's streets today is like moving through layers of time. The ancient Tower of London stands as a silent witness to royal intrigue and executions, while just a short distance away, the gleaming skyscrapers of Canary Wharf reach toward the sky, symbolizing the city's status as one of the world's leading financial centers.

London's cultural significance cannot be overstated. The British Museum houses treasures from civilizations spanning the globe, while the West End theater district rivals Broadway for its world-class productions. The city's parks—Hyde Park, Regent's Park, and countless others—offer green respite from the urban bustle, proving that even in one of the world's busiest cities, nature finds its place.

The Thames itself tells London's story. Once the lifeblood of trade during the height of the British Empire, it now serves as a scenic backdrop for tourists and locals alike, with iconic bridges like Tower Bridge and landmarks such as the London Eye offering stunning views of the ever-evolving skyline.

England's capital continues to reinvent itself while honoring its past. From the traditional changing of the guard at Buckingham Palace to the cutting-edge tech startups emerging in areas like Shoreditch, London embodies a unique duality—deeply rooted in tradition yet constantly pushing toward innovation.

Whether drawn by history, culture, business, or simply the desire to experience one of the world's great cities, visitors to London find themselves immersed in a place that never quite lets go of its past while always looking firmly toward the future.

**Speaker of British House of Commons Resigns Amid Expenses Scandal**

LONDON, England (CNN) — Michael Martin announced his resignation as Speaker of the British House of Commons on Tuesday, becoming the first casualty at the top of British politics in a widening scandal over lawmakers' expense claims that has outraged the British public.

Martin, 63, told the packed chamber that he would step down on June 21, ending a tenure marked by mounting criticism over his handling of the expenses controversy and calls from all sides of the political spectrum for him to go.

"I have decided that I will relinquish the office of speaker on Sunday the 21st of June," Martin told a hushed House of Commons. "This will allow the House to proceed to elect a new speaker on Monday the 22nd of June. I wish my successor here a much easier time than I have had."

The announcement came after days of intense pressure from members of Parliament across party lines who accused Martin of failing to get ahead of the scandal and of focusing his energy on trying to block disclosure of lawmakers' expense claims rather than addressing the underlying abuses.

The scandal erupted last month when Britain's Daily Telegraph newspaper began publishing leaked details of MPs' expense claims, revealing a range of questionable and, in some cases, seemingly absurd expenditures billed to taxpayers. Claims included cleaning of moats, repairs to tennis courts, and even, in one case, a claim for a floating duck house.

The revelations have prompted widespread public fury at a time when Britain is grappling with recession, and have damaged the reputations of politicians from Prime Minister Gordon Brown's governing Labour Party as well as the opposition Conservatives and Liberal Democrats.

Martin, who has served as speaker since 2000, had faced particular criticism for his role in trying to prevent disclosure of the expense records and for what many lawmakers described as a defensive and combative reaction as the scandal grew.

Pressure on Martin intensified last week when a group of MPs took the rare step of tabling a formal motion of no confidence in him, an unprecedented challenge to the authority of the speaker, who traditionally serves as an impartial custodian of the chamber's proceedings.

The speaker's decision to resign marks the first time in more than 300 years that a speaker has been forced from office, according to British parliamentary historians. The last speaker to be removed was Sir John Trevor in 1695, who was found guilty of accepting a bribe.

Prime Minister Brown said Tuesday that the resignation was "an important first step" but insisted that broader reforms to the expenses system were needed to restore public trust in Parliament.

"The public are rightly angry," Brown said. "But what people want now is not just words, but action, and they want to see change."

Conservative Party leader David Cameron, who had publicly called for Martin's departure, said the resignation should pave the way for fundamental reform of how Parliament operates.

"This is a moment for our politics to be transformed," Cameron said. "The public are demanding it, and they are right to demand it."

The scandal has already claimed several political casualties beyond Martin. A number of lawmakers from multiple parties have announced they will not seek re-election, while others have pledged to repay questionable expenses.

Under parliamentary procedure, a new speaker will be elected by secret ballot of all members of Parliament. Several names have already begun circulating as potential successors, though no clear front-runner has yet emerged.

Analysts say the scandal — and Martin's fall — could have lasting implications for British politics, further eroding public confidence in institutions already under strain amid the global financial crisis.

"This is about more than one man," said one political analyst. "This is about a systemic failure that has shaken public trust in Parliament to its core."

Martin, a former sheet metal worker from Glasgow, was the first Roman Catholic to hold the speaker's post since the Reformation. His elevation to the role in 2000 was seen by some as a break from the traditionally patrician nature of the office.

Details of a memorial to mark Martin's departure, along with plans for the election of his successor, are expected to be finalized in the coming days as Parliament seeks to move past the controversy that has consumed British politics for weeks.

— CNN's London bureau contributed to this report.

"The system of allowances has been discredited, and we cannot go on as we are," Brown said, outlining plans for an independent body to oversee MPs' expenses and greater transparency in how public money is spent by lawmakers.

Brown proposed a package of reforms including the creation of an independent regulator for parliamentary expenses, a written code of conduct for MPs, and the power for constituents to recall lawmakers found guilty of financial misconduct.

"The public are demanding change, and they are right to do so," Brown told reporters. "This is a moment of opportunity to modernize how Parliament works and restore public trust."

## Political Fallout Continues

The resignation of Martin, only the second Speaker to be forced from office in modern British history — the last being in 1695 — was seen as a watershed moment, signaling that even the most senior figures in Parliament were not immune to the fallout.

Opposition leader David Cameron welcomed Martin's resignation but pressed for faster and more comprehensive reforms, while Liberal Democrat leader Nick Clegg called for a general election, arguing that the scandal had fundamentally undermined the legitimacy of the current Parliament.

As the political establishment grappled with the scandal's implications, analysts said the affair had exposed deep flaws in a system that had allowed lawmakers considerable latitude in claiming expenses with minimal oversight for years.

The scandal's full political cost remained unclear, with more revelations expected as the Telegraph continued to publish details from its cache of documents in the days ahead.
